slides.sub: Two people can say the same word and mean very different things
slides.title: Room 4: Children
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 9. This room is about children, and it is one where two people can say the same word and mean very different things.

slides.quote: “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit’; yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.’”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. James chapter 4, verses 13 to 15.

“Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit’; yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.’”

slides.title: Not a rule against planning
body: James speaks to people who make confident plans as though tomorrow were theirs to command. His concern is presumption.
slides.narration:
First, what this passage is not. It is not about children, and it is not a rule against planning. James is speaking to people who make confident business plans, a town, a year, a profit, as though tomorrow were theirs to command.

His concern is not planning. It is presumption: speaking as though the future belongs to us. “You do not know what tomorrow will bring.” Our lives, he says, are like a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.

slides.title: Hold your plans with open hands
body: “If the Lord wills.” It is not a formula to avoid honest conversation, and not a reason to plan nothing.
slides.sub: You can plan for children. You cannot control how parenthood unfolds.
slides.narration:
And then his instruction: hold your plans with humility. “If the Lord wills.” That is not a formula to avoid honest conversation, and it is not a reason to plan nothing. It is a way of holding what we plan with open hands.

That is the truth this lesson stands on. You can plan for children. You cannot control how parenthood unfolds.

slides.note: Nothing in the passage suggests that those who struggle to have children, or who face loss, have failed or displeased God.
slides.narration: I want to say that carefully. Nothing in the passage suggests that those who struggle to have children, or who face loss, have failed, or have displeased God. James is speaking about how we hold our plans, not about how God treats people.

slides.title: Reality may not match the picture
body: You may face infertility, miscarriage, complications, disability, loss, or a child whose needs you never imagined. Discuss how you will treat each other then.
slides.narration:
But the wisdom applies. Premarital counselling has to be honest about this, and often is not. You may assume pregnancy will come easily, and it may not. You may face infertility, miscarriage, complications, disability, loss, or a child whose needs you never imagined. Those experiences expose differences you did not know existed: in how you grieve, how you pray, how you cope, what you can afford, and what you believe God is doing.

So do not only discuss the child you hope for. Discuss how you will treat each other when reality does not match the picture.

slides.kicker: Here is how it goes wrong
slides.title: The same yes, different pictures
body: One pictures three children, the other two. One expects a parent at home, the other both working. One expects firm discipline, the other something gentler.
slides.narration:
Here is how it usually goes wrong.

Two people say, “We both want children,” and hold an enormous disagreement without knowing it. They agree on the destination and never discuss the journey. Underneath the yes: one pictures three children and the other has always assumed two. One assumes a parent stays home for the first years. The other assumes both keep working. One expects firm discipline because that is how they were raised. The other believes in something much gentler. One expects grandparents deeply involved. The other wants a self-contained household.

slides.title: Both said yes. Neither said when.
body: “Fairly soon after we marry.” “A few years to ourselves first.”
slides.sub: Name the years, not the vague intention.
slides.narration: Then the question of timing, which catches more couples than any of these. “I’d like children fairly soon after we marry.” “I assumed we’d have a few years to ourselves first.” Both said yes. Neither said when. So name the years, not the vague intention.

slides.title: Meanings drive positions
body: For one, family and continuity. For another, responsibility, pressure, or something closer to fear. These rarely get said out loud.
slides.narration: Sometimes the real disagreement is about what children mean. For one person, they are family, continuity, the point of it all. For another they are responsibility, financial pressure, or something closer to fear. Those meanings drive the practical positions, and they rarely get said out loud.

slides.kicker: Already agreed not to have children?
slides.title: A sentence, not a subject
body: What if one of you changes your mind? What do you say to relatives? What if a pregnancy happens anyway?
slides.narration: And do not skip this room if you have already agreed not to have children. You have agreed a sentence, not a subject. What happens if one of you changes your mind at thirty-eight? What do you say to the relatives who will ask? What if a pregnancy happens anyway? Those questions do not go away.

slides.title: What am I assuming my partner wants when it comes to children?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. What am I assuming my partner wants when it comes to children? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: Teach without humiliation
body: Agree: no hitting, threats, humiliation or shaming.
slides.sub: How was I disciplined, and what would I repeat? What would I do differently?
slides.narration: Now discipline. What do I believe about it? Scripture tells parents not to provoke their children to anger, but to bring them up in the instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). Christian discipline should therefore teach and guide without humiliation or cruelty. Agree to teach boundaries without hitting, threats, humiliation or shaming. And ask the question that reveals more than most: how was I disciplined as a child, and what would I repeat? What would I do differently? Most people find that their firmest parenting convictions came from their own childhood, either as replication or as reaction. Both are worth knowing about before you are holding a tired two-year-old at eleven at night.

slides.title: Children are not projects
body: How would we support one another and seek help if our child had a disability or needs we had not anticipated?
slides.narration: Another question prepares you for the central fact of parenthood: how would we support one another and seek appropriate help if our child had a disability or needs we had not anticipated? Children are not projects you get to specify.

slides.kicker: If you cannot have the children you hoped for
slides.title: Grieve together
body: Do not look for whose fault it is. The quieter one is not indifferent. Conversations about treatment or adoption need compassion, not accusation.
slides.narration: If you are unable to have the children you hoped for, you need to be able to grieve together rather than looking for whose fault it is. Grief does not look the same in two people, and the quieter one is not indifferent. If you come to disagree about treatment, or adoption, or when to stop trying, those conversations need compassion rather than accusation. They are among the hardest a marriage can face.

slides.title: No clean answer
body: You cannot make someone genuinely want to be a parent. A change of mind here can bring profound grief and may create a difference the couple cannot resolve.
slides.narration: Now, one more thing, and it needs to be said plainly, because it happens. One says, “You promised me we’d have children.” The other says, “I know what I said when we were engaged. I don’t feel the same way now.” There is no clean answer to that. You cannot make someone genuinely want to be a parent, and a change of mind here has profound consequences. A change of mind about parenthood can bring profound grief and may create a difference the couple cannot resolve.

slides.title: Do not promise casually
body: Do not make a promise about children because you are afraid of losing the relationship. And do not assume marriage will settle it.
slides.narration: So here is the instruction for right now: do not make a promise about children casually because you are afraid of losing the relationship. That is the people-pleasing from Lesson 1, applied to the highest-stakes subject available. And do not assume that marriage will settle it, that if you say yes now you will come to mean it, or that they will come round.

slides.kicker: One definitely wants, one definitely does not
slides.title: Not a problem to fix after the wedding
body: It may be a genuine incompatibility, worth facing while facing it is still possible.
slides.narration: If one of you definitely wants children and the other definitely does not, that is not a communication problem to be worked out after the wedding. It may be a genuine incompatibility, and it deserves to be faced honestly while facing it is still possible. Seek help to understand your choices, not to pressure either person into parenthood.

slides.kicker: If one of you is unsure
slides.title: Ask what the uncertainty means
body: Do not assume it is fear to be overcome. Allow honest uncertainty, and avoid persuasion disguised as reassurance.
slides.narration: If one of you is simply unsure, ask what the uncertainty means without assuming it is fear to be overcome. It may reflect priorities, health, ambivalence or a wish not to parent. Allow honest uncertainty and avoid persuasion disguised as reassurance.

body: “We don’t know what parenthood will bring. Whatever comes, we will not turn on each other because it didn’t match what we imagined.”
slides.narration: Where you are united in wanting children, the most useful preparation is not agreeing about names or schools. It is being able to say, and mean: “We don’t know what parenthood will bring. Whatever comes, we will not turn on each other because it didn’t match what we imagined.”

slides.title: About twenty minutes
list: Do I want to become a parent, or am I uncertain?
What do I imagine children will bring?
Am I afraid of anything about becoming a parent?
How was I disciplined, and what would I keep?
slides.sub: You do not have to write anything down.
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, about twenty minutes alone with the questions in the worksheet. Do I want to become a parent, not plan to become a parent, or am I uncertain? What do I imagine children will bring? Am I afraid of anything about becoming a parent? How was I disciplined, and what would I keep? What would I never repeat? You do not have to write anything down.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes
list: Do we want to become parents, and is either of us uncertain?
What timing and family size do we presently imagine?
Am I saying yes because I mean it, or because I fear losing this relationship?
slides.note: If you feel uncertain, name it now. Uncertainty must not be presented as agreement.
slides.narration:
Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, together, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Work through three main questions. First: do we want to become parents, and is either of us uncertain? Second: what timing and family size do we presently imagine? Name the years, not the vague intention. Third, and it is the honest one, out loud: am I saying yes because I genuinely mean it, or because I fear losing this relationship?

If you feel uncertain, name it honestly now. You do not need immediate certainty, but uncertainty must not be presented as agreement.

slides.title: Record where you are
body: Choose which conversations to continue: work and childcare, discipline, and what you will do if it does not go to plan. Record each person’s present position. List any advice you need.
slides.narration:
There are other important conversations: work and childcare, discipline, and what you will do if it does not go to plan. You do not need to finish them today. Choose which you will continue, and when.

Before you leave, record each person’s present position on children and timing. Do not treat uncertainty as agreement. And list any information or professional advice you need.

body: Lord, we hold our plans before You. Give us honesty about what we want and what we fear. If children come, make us gentle. If they do not, or if the way is hard, keep us from turning on each other. Teach us to say “If the Lord wills,” without losing our courage to speak the truth. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, we hold our plans before You. Give us honesty about what we want and what we fear. If children come, make us gentle. If they do not, or if the way is hard, keep us from turning on each other. Teach us to say “If the Lord wills,” without losing our courage to speak the truth. Amen.

slides.title: Lesson 10
slides.narration: I’ll see you in Lesson 10.
